newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Yugoslavia sanctions to be lifted soon - officials.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia sanctions to be lifted soon - officials.

text.p: Western government ministers on Thursday said U.N. sanctions against rump Yugoslavia would be lifted soon, following the Sept. 14 elections in Bosnia.

They spoke after the United States, key European allies and Russia met to discuss how to shore up peace in Bosnia following the vote to elect joint institutions to run the multi-ethnic state foreseen in the Dayton peace accord.

"I think there was agreement right 'round the table that the conditions laid down in Dayton have been broadly satisfied and that it's appropriate for the sanctions to be lifted pretty soon," British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said.
"I think it's days we're talking about, not weeks," Rifkind told reporters.

The United Nations imposed the sanctions in 1992 because of Serbia's role in fomenting the Bosnian war. They were suspended after last year's Dayton, Ohio, peace agreement but have yet to be formally lifted.

Foreign ministers from the five-nation "contact group" on former Yugoslavia and peace coordinator Carl Bildt met at the U.S. Mission to the United Nations on the margins of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. The contact group comprises the United States, Russia, France, Germany and Britain.

Participants said the U.N. Security Council could not lift the sanctions until the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which supervised the elections, had certified that they met the standards laid down by Dayton. But French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said he expected this within 48 hours.

Bildt, who was to brief the U.N. Security Council on Bosnia developments later in the day, said he wanted the council to specify that it was ready to reimpose sanctions if necessary. This could be done "against anyone that would undertake actions that would threaten the unity of Bosnia-Herzegovina or in other ways seriously jeopardise the implementation of the peace agreement," he told reporters.

Bosnia's Serbs and Croats are widely suspected of wanting to merge the parts of Bosnia they control with Serbia and Croatia, respectively, at some point in the future, although the Dayton accord forbids them to do so.

There was no comment from U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who was meeting successively with Bosnia's Moslem President Alija Izetbegovic, Serbian Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic and Croatian Foreign Minister Mate Granic.

The United States has been the country most reluctant to lift sanctions and says it plans to keep its own "outer wall" of sanctions to bar rump Yugoslavia -- Serbia and Montenegro - - from access to international financial institutions.

Rifkind said he had been told by Izetbegovic that the three-man collective Bosnia presidency elected this month -- Izetbegovic, Serb Momcilo Krajisnik and Croat Kresimir Zubak -- could hold its first meeting on Monday. Other officials said no date had been set but a meeting was expected next week.

Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, representing the European Union, said there had been no discussion of an international peacekeeping force to replace the NATO-led IFOR implementation force, whose mandate expires in December.

But he said: "I think there is a general view emerging from all of our discussions in New York this week that there will have to be a new post-IFOR mandate. The shape of that or the actual scale of it has not been discussed in any detail yet."
The issue is sensitive in the United States because of presidential elections Nov. 5. President Bill Clinton has promised that U.S. troops in IFOR will come home this year.
